newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank more pragmatic, sticks to EMU date.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank more pragmatic, sticks to EMU date.

text.p: The Bundesbank may be taking a softer, more pragmatic approach on the fiscal criteria for European monetary union, insisting that the 1999 launch date must be met, economists said on Tuesday.
On a strict interpretation, Germany, the driving force behind integration, might itself miss key economic targets for union due to the impact of high unemployment.

But as officials of the German central bank step up public speaking engagements to tell a sceptical public about the benefits of currency union, hard-line views on fulfilling all criteria exactly appear to have been toned down.
What remains is Germany's insistence that the launch must go ahead as planned at the end of the decade but only with nations that can maintain stability in the long term.

Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm, who is also president of the state central bank in Baden Wuerttemberg, on Monday said talk of delaying the start of a single European currency was "totally misplaced".

Postponing the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) would lead to an immediate, sharp rise in the mark, which would hurt German exports and stunt nations' efforts to achieve a further consolidation of finances, Palm and several colleagues said.

But at the same time Palm and council members Ernst Welteke and Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said the European Union's goal for cutting budget deficits to qualify for EMU was only one of a number of entry criteria and possibly not the most instrumental for sustaining a stable union.

Economists said this emphasis appears to be gaining the upper hand now as hardliners like Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum and council members like Reimut Jochimsen have been strangely silent.
"It is interesting that these are not the people making headlines these days," said Ralf Kugelstadt, economist at UBS in Frankfurt. "It would be interesting to hear what these people have to say."

Apart from the deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the EU's Maastricht Treaty states that participating nations must show stable foreign exchange rates and long-term interest and inflation rates. Many more nations already fulfil these goals.

"In my opinion European currency union can start in January 1999 while conforming to those EMU convergence criteria that are most often discussed," said Welteke, also president of the state central bank in Hesse.
Bundesbank officials are starting to question how a budget deficit of just under three percent could be good for stability while one of slightly over three percent would be negative.
"The three percent deficit criteria should not be a knock-out criteria", prohibiting any nation just over that level from entering, Welteke said.

Fearing strict entry goals could give way to creative book-keeping, Palm said, "A trick-free deficit of just over three percent in 1997 that will be further reduced in following years due to savings efforts is preferable to 2.9 percent reached through creative accounting."
Germany, once Europe's star economic performer, stands perilously close to missing the EMU entry criteria, threatening to keep Europe's biggest economy outside the union.

While the Bonn government sticks by forecasts that the 1997 deficit will be at 2.9 percent of GDP, independent economists said this would be highly unlikely considering Germany's record high jobless levels, standing at 4.7 million people.

Economists said it was reassuring that Bundesbank officials, while toning down comments about EMU criteria, left no doubt that the central bank was as inflation-conscious as ever, insisting that it would take the appropriate action if price pressures intensified.
